vignette: Diane’s life fractured during a late autumn evening when a man ambushed her in the hospital parking garage. The attacker had pinned her left wrist and pressed his knee against her ribs, his breath hot against her neck as he demanded her purse. She had come to believe that any discussion of future plans now mirrored that absolute loss of control, and she was certain that simply recounting the event would fracture her composure. When her daughter mentioned upcoming travel dates or a former colleague brought up the case file over coffee, Diane’s mind instantly supplied the visceral memory of the attack. The raw images of her wrists being gripped and the sounds of the struggle flooded her awareness, making it impossible to continue the conversation. Each time the memory intruded, she interpreted her racing heart and shaking hands as proof that she was fundamentally inadequate, permanently stripping her of the happiness she once cherished. Her conviction that she would collapse if she processed the trauma caused her to push the memory away before it could fully form, leaving only fragmented, emotionless echoes as if she were watching a stranger’s life unfold. Because she was convinced she would not be able to handle the event if she thought about it, Diane adopted rigid physical routines to manage the threat. She never exercised, preferring to conserve her strength, and at the precinct she always sat with her back against the wall so she could monitor the doorway. The intense rage that flared whenever she remembered the garage assault drove her to implement these boundaries; she restricted her food intake because eating felt like a luxury she could not afford while remaining hyper-alert. Yet by starving herself and avoiding movement, she inadvertently kept her nervous system in a state of perpetual readiness, which meant the trauma memory never settled into a coherent narrative. Her rigid routines and physical withdrawal convinced her that she could no longer function normally, reinforcing the appraisal that she was inadequate and permanently stripped of joy. Because she was certain that discussing future plans or the assault itself was unbearable, she became hyper-vigilant to those exact topics, interpreting casual conversation as a direct threat. The physical tension from never exercising and the constant scanning required by sitting with her back to a wall left her nerves frayed, so even minor references to the event or future plans triggered an immediate, disproportionate alarm. Now, at seventy-one, Diane’s days are spent sifting through decades of forensic evidence in a climate-controlled records room, a job that once felt like a calling but now functions as a daily gauntlet. She avoids walking to her car because the open asphalt reminds her of the garage, and she routinely skips lunch breaks because the idea of sitting down feels like surrender. When her supervisor asked her to lead a briefing on upcoming case reviews, the prospect of discussing future timelines triggered a wave of nausea that mirrored the attacker’s suffocating grip. Diane finally sought therapy because the isolation had become unbearable; she was terrified that without intervention, she would continue to misinterpret every future conversation as a prelude to violence, and she desperately hoped to reclaim the ability to trust her own mind again.
